questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/43c8d1ced440e0fe79052c1329ff3af865e1fdbfb4cc0c7ad0a9c176592358e9.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,1)$ to the point $(2,2),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,t+1⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,1)$ and $(2,2).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(1+t(2-1))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,t+1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-1)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)+(t+1)^{2} \\  & =(3t-1)+({t}^{2}+2t+1) \\  & ={t}^{2}+5t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+5t)\cdot 3\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+5t)\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $4,$ traversed from the point $(-4,0)$ to the point $(4,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-16{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $16{x}^{2}+25{y}^{2}=400,$ traversed from the point $(0,-4)$ to the point $(5,0),$ as shown above?
*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x-y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-5{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}y{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $2,$ traversed from the point $(0,2)$ to the point $(-2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*

We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=y{e}^{x},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot {e}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot {e}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{e}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3,$ traversed from the point $(0,\sqrt{3})$ to the point $(0,-\sqrt{3}),$ as shown above?

We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,-2)$ to the point $(2,4),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,-2)$ and $(2,4).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(-2+t(4-(-2)))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-2)=6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)\cdot (6t-2) \\  & =18{t}^{2}-12t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(18{t}^{2}-12t+2)\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-6t+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,-1)$ to the point $(2,1),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,2t-1⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,-1)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(-1+t(1-(-1)))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,2t-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)^{2}-(2t-1) \\  & =9{t}^{2}-6t+1-2t+1 \\  & =9{t}^{2}-8t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-8t+2)\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-8t+2)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $16{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=64,$ traversed from the point $(-2,0)$ to the point $(2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =12{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12 \\  & =4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/cb4c4828626255e26e298a0cdc202b37852df9d39bcfe15e0e67d350d90f774a.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(2,2),$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(2,0)$ and $(2,2).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(2+t(2-2)),\,(0+t(2-0))⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})+{x}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi (2t)}{2})+(2)^{2} \\  & =\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t+4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t+4)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(4+\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2(4t-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2[(4-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )-(0-\operatorname{cos}⁡0)] \\  & =2[4-(-1)+1] \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}{8y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+16(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{16({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =-8{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8t\,{|}_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =-8(\frac{3\pi }{2}-\pi ) \\  & =-8(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}\frac{1}{2}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the upper half of the circle of radius $2,$ traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(-2,0),$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a half of a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =4{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}[(1)^{3}-(-1)^{3}] \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}x{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the three-quarters of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(3,0),$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $3$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t){e}^{1-{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t{e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t{e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t})\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t{e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u={cos}^{2}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t{e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =-9{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{u}\,(-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{e}^{u}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}[{e}^{1}-{e}^{0}] \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\cdot (e-1) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(e-1)\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/dfa95100566fce9ab113b00ae53d1a76e8977b68aa4bac0e9b6892a9930b70d4.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}\frac{y{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}}{8x}\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the lower half of the circle of radius $4,$ traversed from the point $(-4,0)$ to the point $(4,0),$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{y{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}}{8x},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{3}}{8(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{64\operatorname{sin}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}{32\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }2\operatorname{tan}⁡t\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =-8[\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ] \\  & =-8(1-(-1)) \\  & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/4b5c788ad2c220b70a7f1d333680a70933f9b490a0db11fb3440dd3a2e06fa01.png)

Find a definite integral that's equivalent to the line integral $\displaystyle \int_C (x+y) \, \textrm{d} x,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(3,3),$ as shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}x  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(0,0)$ and $(3,3).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0+t(3-0),\,0+t(3-0)⟩ \\  & =⟨3t,\,3t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \le t \le 1.$

Computing $\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x+y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3t+3t \\  & =6t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6t\cdot 3\,\text{d}t \\  & =18{\int }_{0}^{1}t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the definite integral equivalent to the line integral $\displaystyle\int_C x^2 \, \textrm d y,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $25x^2 + 4y^2 = 100,$ traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,5),$ as shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 5\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Computing $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}=4{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(4{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot 5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =20{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_C \left(x^2 + y^2\right)\,\textrm d y,$ where $C$ is the path along the upper-right quarter of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 4,$ traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,2),$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/8fc3a36829c9780c34e13f253d607c3849bfd3ef1399a77a79a3dd3d30ef7140.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a quarter of a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 2\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Computing $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =4({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-8\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$
